metaData.originalTitle: 2026：软件的末日、工程师的陨落、平庸的消失
metaData.title: 2026: The End of Software, the Fall of Engineers, the Disappearance of Mediocrity
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: Using the sharp decline in US software stocks in early 2026 as a starting point, this article deeply analyzes how AI Agents are eroding the SaaS middle-layer business model, and explores structural shifts in software form from product to medium, and the engineer's role from writing code to understanding systems.
metaData.summary: The article uses the January 2026 US software stock crash (SaaSpocalypse) as a starting point, pointing out that AI Agents are fundamentally shaking the SaaS business model. Core arguments include: 1) AI bypasses traditional software interfaces via APIs, eroding the SaaS middle layer (e.g., Thomson Reuters, Atlassian) whose moat was built on interfaces and usage habits, while underlying systems involving compliance and auditing (e.g., ERP) remain relatively stable due to high switching costs; 2) The total amount of software will not decrease; instead, the exponential drop in token costs (Jevons Paradox) will spawn more new software, with software transforming from a fixed product to an on-demand generated medium; 3) The Agent era requires rebuilding three layers of infrastructure: protocols (MCP), payments (x402), and distribution (browse.sh); 4) Entry-level engineering positions are being squeezed by AI, but value is shifting from writing code to understanding systems, giving rise to the new role of FDE (Forward Deployed Engineer). The article comprehensively cites viewpoints from a16z, Benedict Evans, Noah Smith, and others, with detailed data and rigorous logic.

mainPoints.point: AI Agents are eroding the SaaS middle-layer business model, with companies whose moat is built on interfaces and usage habits being the first to suffer.
mainPoints.explanation: AI accesses backend data directly via APIs, bypassing traditional software interfaces. The companies being heavily shorted by the market are those whose value is concentrated in the 'top 80%' middle-layer businesses easily replicable by AI, such as legal information services and project management tools.

mainPoints.point: The total amount of software will not decrease due to AI; instead, it will spawn more new software due to falling token costs (Jevons Paradox).
mainPoints.explanation: Token prices have dropped over 99% in two years, but total consumption has risen exponentially. Cheaper tokens unlock previously non-existent software scenarios, such as Vibe Coding and OpenDesign, transforming software from a fixed product to an on-demand generated medium.

mainPoints.point: The Agent era requires rebuilding three layers of infrastructure: protocols, payments, and distribution, with MCP, x402, and browse.sh being typical examples.
mainPoints.explanation: MCP standardizes the connection between AI and external tools (analogous to a USB interface), x402 enables machine-native instant payments, and platforms like browse.sh distribute Agent capabilities like npm.

mainPoints.point: Entry-level engineering positions are being squeezed by AI, but value is shifting from 'writing code' to 'understanding systems,' giving rise to the new FDE role.
mainPoints.explanation: Employment rates for junior developers aged 22-25 in the US have dropped nearly 20%, but demand for senior developers has increased. FDEs (Forward Deployed Engineers) require an intersection of engineering, product, and customer skills, responsible for making AI systems actually work within enterprises.

keyQuotes: The emergence of AI agents is fundamentally shaking this foundation.
Software is no longer a craftsman's work; it is a medium that can be generated on demand.
What is dying here is precisely the middle-layer SaaS, whose value is mostly concentrated in the upper layer, with little compliance substance underneath.

Software is not dead; it has simply transformed from a product into a medium. Geeks have not disappeared either; they have just evolved from people who write code into people who make systems actually work.
Code generated by AI will have bugs and architectural flaws. Knowing where the problem lies and why it occurs requires not faster generation speed, but deeper understanding.
